newsitem.title: USA: Congressional analyst sees lower 1997 deficit.
newsitem.headline: Congressional analyst sees lower 1997 deficit.

text.p: Congressional Budget Office deputy director Jim Blum said he expects the current fiscal year 1997 deficit in the range of $30 billion to $40 billion and the 1998 deficit to be just slightly larger.

Blum said tax revenues had been much higher than expected this year accounting for the improvements over CBO's May forecast of a $67 billion fiscal 1997 deficit. Wall St. analysts put the deficit for 1997 under $50 billion and some lawmakers have predicted it could be closer to $30 billion.
"There has been a whole lot more income out there than we had discerned," he said. The same situation is occurring in state governments, he noted.

The deficit in the 1998 fiscal year which starts Oct. 1 should rise slightly above the 1997 figure, Blum noted, due to the tax cuts which take effect in 1998. The Joint Committee on Taxation forecast a net $9 billion tax cut in fiscal 1998.

CBO will issue its next official estimate of the fiscal 1997 deficit and its outlook for coming years in mid-September. Around that time the White House's Office of Management and Budget is to issue its mid-session review which is expected to also show an improvement in the fiscal 1997 deficit estimate.
The Clinton administration is on record with a $125 billion deficit for 1997.

The Treasury Department reported last week the federal deficit shriveled to $10.87 billion for the first nine months of the 1997 fiscal yaer. During the same nine month period of the 1996 fiscal year the deficit was $74 billion.
Blum said the five year balanced budget bill passed by Congress Thursday would achieve its goal of balancing government spending and revenues by 2002.
